title: Are You Immune To Changing?
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston summarizes Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey's Immunity to Change, which distills 25 years of Harvard research into why leaders and organizations struggle to make changes they say they want. He opens with the statistic that only one in nine high-risk heart patients makes the recommended lifestyle changes even under threat of death. The authors' explanation is an emotional immune system that protects the status quo from the anticipated dangers of change, driven by competing commitments and a hidden "Big Assumption". A case study of a CEO who could not delegate shows that his goal clashed with a belief that delegating leaders are lazy and selfish, so delegation skills alone could never solve it. Houston distinguishes technical from adaptive challenges and lays out steps for an immunity map: write the goal, list counter-productive behaviors, identify competing commitments and surface the Big Assumption, then run small experiments to test it, ideally with a coach.
points: People often cannot change because they hold competing commitments, like having a foot on the gas and the brake at the same time.
The CEO case shows that a goal such as delegating more can fail because it contradicts a core belief about what a real leader does.
Technical training cannot fix an adaptive challenge; the underlying belief must be reframed before skills can take hold.
The immunity map has five steps, ending with surfacing the Big Assumption that quietly protects the old behavior.
Small, low-pressure experiments that test the assumption, supported by a coach or mentor, are more realistic than trying to change permanently at once.
quotes: We all have a kind of emotional immune system that protects us from the anticipated potential negative effects of change. The job of your emotional immune system is to keep the status quo and protect you from the emotional dangers that might result from you making significant changes in your life.
Despite a stern warning—change or die—patients still could not change their diet and exercise habits.
Kegan and Lahey help people examine the competing commitments that may be in direct conflict with the goals they set.
Changing our behavior is surprisingly difficult because our core beliefs are often the result of deeply ingrained behaviors that arise from childhood emotional survival strategies.
He was not aware that he ultimately believed that leaders who delegated things were “lazy and selfish, and dumped their responsibilities on the people that worked under them.
No amount of teaching delegation skills (technical skills) was going to change David’s behavior.
The idea of experimenting is essential here because it’s easier to say you are experimenting than to put the pressure on yourself to immediately change your behavior and make it permanent right away.
